posts.heading: September 13, 2026
posts.text:
The Tufted Titmouse arrived two minutes before sunrise, maintaining a steady rhythm of visits until nearly two hours after light. By 07:43, a Carolina Chickadee joined the rotation, while the Northern Cardinal dominated the early auditory landscape with twenty-two detections in the seventh hour.

The first confident visual record of a House Finch at this station came when an adult male perched on the top ring of the metal stand.

By 10:30, seventy visits had been recorded, more than double the recent average of thirty-four. Thirteen species were accounted for, surpassing the usual seven.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged its busiest day of the week, with 88 feeder visits and 11 species recorded. This volume more than doubles the average of 43 visits over the previous week, extending the high activity levels seen on Thursday and Friday. Regulars such as Tufted Titmice, Carolina Chickadees, and Mourning Doves maintained their presence, while the absence of the Red-shouldered Hawk and Northern Mockingbird marks a slight shift in the species mix compared to recent days.

Mourning Dove was heard for the first time at this station. The station also recorded its first confident visual of a Northern Cardinal approaching a treat bowl. These auditory and visual firsts align with the recent expansion of the feeder station, which included the addition of nectar, seed, and treat feeders starting on Monday.

Tufted Titmice remained the dominant species, accounting for 49 visits throughout the daylight hours. Their first appearance occurred 38 minutes after sunrise, and their final visit was logged 660 minutes after sunrise.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The afternoon quiet ended with a distinct evening surge, as Carolina Wrens logged nine additional detections and American Crows added three in the 19:00 hour. This final burst brought the day's total to one hundred and three feeder visits, significantly exceeding the recent average of thirty-three.

The last visual record of the day belongs to an American Crow, seen seven hundred and nine minutes after sunrise near the water bowl. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees maintained their dominance at the feeders, while the American Goldfinch remains the station’s first confident visual record of the species.

The sound and sight counts reflect a busier day than the recent norm, with the Wren’s persistent chorus bridging the gap from early morning calls to the final dusk detections.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The day closed with ninety total feeder visits, a volume that dwarfs the seven recorded in recent evenings. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees sustained a steady presence, keeping the station active well past the recent daily average. The auditory record remains dense, with two hundred and twenty-one vocal detections surpassing the recent average of one hundred and seven, driven by the persistent Carolina Wren and American Crow.

The final visual contact of the day came at 18:36, a Northern Mockingbird registering seventy-four minutes before sunset. The station’s activity level today stands in sharp contrast to the quiet of recent days, which averaged only six species and seven visits up to this hour.

As dusk settles, the air is quiet save for the lingering calls of the Carolina Wren and the distant caw of the American Crow. The day’s total of thirteen species marks a significant increase over the recent average of six.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The station closed with its busiest activity in the past week, recording 23 feeder visits and 11 species, a sharp contrast to the five preceding days which averaged zero visual sightings. The high count aligns with the installation of a nectar feeder and a tube seed feeder on September 7. These three species, along with the Carolina Chickadee and Blue Jay, were not recorded during the previous week, marking a significant expansion in the visual log.

The Ruby-throated Hummingbird made the first confident visual appearance of the day, appearing 274 minutes after sunrise. By the end of the day, the Northern Mockingbird provided the last clear sighting, perched on a wire 20 minutes before sunset.

The Blue Jay and Red-bellied Woodpecker led the late-day detections, adding to the day's total of 238 vocal records. This surge in both visual and audio data stands out against the recent quiet period, where detection averages hovered around 42.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
Yesterday’s 79 detections stood in sharp contrast to the five recorded on Monday, with the six species detected marking a significant jump from the single day of activity earlier this week. While the station remained visually silent with no feeder visits, the auditory log captured a full day of sound, led by Red-bellied Woodpeckers and Carolina Wrens.

The activity spread across the day rather than clustering in a single burst, a departure from the brief vocalizations recorded on Monday. Red-shouldered Hawks were heard in the late morning, adding to the roster of species recorded on this site for the first time.

New feeders installed on the pole on Monday were not visited during the day, keeping the physical log empty despite the high volume of calls. The day’s total reflects a sustained presence of sound, with Eastern Towhees and Blue Jays contributing to the final counts as the light faded.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
The station logged its first day of data, recording five audio detections and no visual contacts. This marks the first recorded activity for the Carolina Wren and the Eastern Towhee at this location.

Two feeders were installed and refilled during the evening, adding nectar and seed options. The new hardware did not prompt any visual visits from the two species heard.
